# Weaknesses and Future Work

## Weaknesses

Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the present findings.
Most fundamentally, the design of the present study did not incorporate
a ground-truth measure of emotional state against which the derived
labels could be validated. Valence and arousal labels are instead
derived from two independent proxy measures, facial expression via
HSEmotion and HRV via RMSSD respectively, rather than from validated
psychological assessments. Because these channels are measured
independently and combined only after processing, any inaccuracy
specific to either channel propagates directly into the resulting
emotion label, without a means of cross-validation between them.

Construct validity represents a related concern. HSEmotion achieves only
around 55-70% accuracy in benchmark evaluations [@savchenko2022],
implying that a non-trivial proportion of valence labels may be
misclassified independently of any plant signal. The arousal axis is
narrow in the same way: it rests on two HRV measures whose validity at
lower arousal levels is well documented as limited [@choi2017], which is
reflected in the comparatively weak arousal classification result.

The stimulus itself constitutes a further limitation. The video used to
elicit emotional responses was reused from an earlier, unrelated COIN
seminar project [@schafer2025], rather than being validated specifically
for the present study using a standardized emotion induction protocol
such as IAPS or a comparable normed stimulus set. Its capacity to
reliably elicit the intended range of valence and arousal states across
a heterogeneous participant sample was therefore not independently
confirmed.

The sample size of 15 participants, yielding 284 analyzable windows,
results in comparatively wide confidence intervals, particularly evident
in the arousal classification result. This limits the statistical power
to detect smaller effects and constrains the precision of the reported
effect size estimates. Relatedly, the correlation analysis evaluated 22
plant-derived features across two complementary analysis variants
without applying a correction for multiple comparisons, which should be
taken into account when interpreting the reported significance levels.

The experimental setup itself imposes additional constraints. As in
Gloor [@gloor2025], a single plant species (*Kalanchoe*) was used throughout all
recording sessions. Consequently, the extent to which the observed
plant-valence association generalizes across different plant species or
individual specimens remains untested. Unlike Gloor [@gloor2025], the present
study did not include sham or shielding controls, such as electrodes
attached to a non-living conductor or recordings inside a Faraday cage,
to rule out the possibility that classification performance is partly
driven by electromagnetic artifacts rather than genuine plant
physiology. Furthermore, all sessions were conducted on a single day in
a room that was not otherwise isolated from external environmental
influences. While this ensured that broad conditions such as outdoor
weather remained comparatively constant across sessions, factors such as
room temperature, humidity, and air movement were neither held constant
nor systematically recorded. Their precise influence on the plant signal
therefore cannot be determined from the present data.

## Future Work

Several directions follow from these findings. First, the comparison
with Gloor [@gloor2025] suggests that the lower accuracy observed here is more
plausibly attributable to a more conservative and generalizable
evaluation framework, namely grouped cross-validation across 15
participants and permutation testing, than to a weaker underlying effect. Future
studies should build on this by using larger and more diverse
participant samples to narrow the wide confidence intervals observed for
arousal and emotion classification, ideally under professionally
controlled laboratory conditions with stable air quality, humidity, and
temperature, so as to minimize session-level environmental drift and
isolate the physiological signal of interest more effectively.

Second, operationalizing emotion via the dimensional valence-arousal
model [@russell1980] revealed differential sensitivity across affective
dimensions that would likely have remained obscured under a combined
categorical label. Valence and arousal should therefore be treated as
analytically distinct constructs and modeled as separate targets with
dimension-specific refinements: alternative HRV-based markers for
arousal could be evaluated beyond RMSSD, given its documented
limitations [@choi2017], and higher-performing FER models than HSEmotion
could be tested for valence. Complementing the physiological channels
with validated self-report instruments such as the Self-Assessment
Manikin [@bradleylang1994] may further strengthen interpretation,
provided such measures are used in addition to, rather than instead of,
the physiological channels employed here.

Third, environmental variables such as CO~2~ should be recorded
explicitly and controlled statistically, an issue that has received
little attention in research on plant bioelectrical signals; the present
analysis indicates that CO~2~ does not confound the plant-valence
relationship. Future studies could extend this by including volatile
organic compound (VOC) measurements alongside CO~2~ to assess whether
other airborne chemical signals mediate or confound the plant-emotion
relationship in ways that CO~2~ alone cannot capture.

Fourth, the finding that level-invariant and session-relative features,
above all the Hjorth dynamics descriptors, consistently outranked
absolute-level features contributes to feature engineering in
this domain and helps explain why session-normalized features tend to
yield better performance. Future work could investigate this pattern
using more precise, higher-resolution plant bioelectrical sensors, which
may improve the signal-to-noise ratio and reveal finer temporal dynamics
than the current AD8232-based setup permits.
